searchText: Well, I guess that's fine. I will open prs to update in repo the main other blocker i have is really around binary data representation. there was talk about using standard base64 formatting, but then there's also things like 'root' in routes, which wouldn't be able to be base64 (some of the characters are invalid for a route) is there any resolution on using hex representations vs base64? According to call notes of api call, "there was strong sentiment against base64". Most of clients are already using hex because of readability (block explorers and logs are displaying everything as hex) it sounded like prysm was fairly adamant thats all... but all good i'll stick with hex i was trying to find references but there wasn't much, it saves me implementing more serializers so that works 🙂 at prysm we were just using base64 to align with some common standards, but consensus is on hex strings Otherwise theres no differentiation between string representations of bytes values vs just strings yep the standards thing is understandable, i guess that's where the question came from, i was just hoping the answer wasnt hex in routes and b64 in json No worries, there wont be a mix of both thanks <@!545555441518772225> and <@!311971895828283393> i really appreciate the information It was also painful for us in Go to have to support bytes values as hex strings in our api, which was part of our rationale for base64 standard > It was also painful for us in Go to have to support bytes values as hex strings in our api, which was part of our rationale for base64 standard <@311971895828283393> out of curiosity, do you use base64 without padding or do you escape it in url? noone was using params in url as far as i saw, which is why it was probably not a problem well query params quoted strings in query params is fine, just in url its sticky and needs encoding Im not entirely sure <@545555441518772225> would have to check the output of an endpoint in https://api.prylabs.network, it just returns the format the grpc json gateway outputs `https://api.prylabs.net/eth/v1alpha1/beacon/blocks?root=fQ602Djcrb1un3Wf8DTYOVOBiSG1ei8V0U1uBSmGZnM%3D ` uri encoded - the %3D Theres an ongoing api standardization effort <@680234424037670912> , so our api currently doesnt match other clients, but we’ll all work towards that goal in the future yep that's ok, that's what i'm also working towards 🙂 hence the random questions, so i appreciate both of your time There are options in-between base 16 and base 64... Like base 32, for example (if you want to keep byte aligned). Base 36 if you want a bit more bang for your buck while still getting maximal compatibility and you don't mind losing 8-bit alignment. Hex strings (with a `0x` prefix) seem to be simple and sane. They are used by community tools (e.g. etherscan, beaconcha.in, eth1 tools) in various places, with as far as I've seen no pushback. Going with a format that we already recognize seems like the best option, certainly if the alternatives are there mainly to save a few bytes here and there. Base 32 (I think) addresses are used in Bitcoin without pushback. "Save a few bytes here and there" is more like "save an order of magnitude bytes everywhere" when talking about the JSON-RPC (for example). *everything* in the ETH 1.x JSON-RPC API is base-16 blobs. A base 32 blob is half the space, base 64 1/4 the space. FWIW, JS supports radix up to 36 for serializing `bigint`. We will eventually enable ssz response in case you wan't to save bytes. But the api is designed not to respond with everything so there are specific endpoints for some common stuff I would personally like to see Base64 just for the visual inspection compression. https://simpleserialize.com/ if you wan't to see ssz decompressed 🙂 When looking at Etherscan and you are presented with a 256-bit value (e.g., blockhash) or 160-bit value (address) they are very long and about 1/3 of the way through I become exhausted and give up. 😛 <@545555441518772225> Is it intended that the "Serialized" field is a base-10 array when output type is base64? I think you should open issue https://github.com/chainsafe/simpleserialize.com. I think you are only one that switched to base64 view 🤣 🎉 <https://github.com/ChainSafe/simpleserialize.com/issues/15> Another selling point with base64 is that a human can get equal probability of differentiating two addresses by looking at fewer characters. I personally have 3 randomly generated accounts that start with the same 3 characters (dumb luck, not vanity addresses). With base64 they would all differ on the first character. > "Save a few bytes here and there" is more like "save an order of magnitude bytes everywhere" when talking about the JSON-RPC (for example). <@!301186049323958275> eh? We're talking about hex strings in URLs and responses, which are a subset of the total data, so even a reduction to 25% wouldn't give huger overall savings. If space was our primary concern we wouldn't have gone with JSON in the first place 🙂 tbh, for me it's harder to compare base64, I think it's because of larger set of possible characters and uneven spacing in typography. I'm trying to find some case study on that. About space saving, let's assume that most of node will be behind some proxy that will gzip content. Base64 will yield a lot worse compressions as oppose to hex which will negate those saved bytes with encoding^^ _pulls out his list of hills he is currently dying on... realizes that he already has a mountain range to deal with and decides to peacefully walk away._ (If it makes you feel better I was rooting for GRPC, so...)
